quote: I realize now that when I wrote “You cannot make yourself believe the sky is green by an act of will,” I wasn’t just a dispassionate reporter of the existing facts. I was also trying to instill a self-fulfilling prophecy.
content: The Litany of Tarski forbids believing something false for its benefits. It does not forbid holding a true belief that also has good consequences. "You cannot make yourself believe the sky is green by an act of will" is true, and Fable grants doxastic involuntarism in the next essay's note. The belief is also partly self-fulfilling: holding it makes it more true. Believing a proposition whose truth is strengthened by your believing it is accurate belief, not belief in belief. Wood et al. tested global self-worth statements ("I am a lovable person") in people with low self-esteem, who found them implausible, and the backfire ran through that implausibility. A reader of this book finds "I can't just decide to believe" plausible. The essay also states its motive openly, which is not how self-deception behaves.

quote: Shouldn’t the gut-level realization, “Oh, wait, the sky really isn’t green” follow from the realization “My map that says ‘the sky is green’ has no reason to be correlated with the territory”?
content: The sequence never promised that knowledge of a map's origin propagates automatically. Book II argues the opposite at length: we change our minds less often than we think, and knowing about biases can hurt. What it claims is that explaining the mechanism, and then practising, does work, and the study Fable cites is the evidence. Ross, Lepper & Hubbard found that ordinary debriefing left the discredited belief in place, and that "process debriefing," which explained the perseverance mechanism itself, largely eliminated it (Ross, Lepper & Hubbard 1975). Explaining how the map fails to track the territory is what makes the correction take. The "chant" is that explanation, made into something one rehearses.
